title: Fear from the rod
hook: fear is born from taking up the rod; see the fish in shrinking water
tomorrow: The way to the far shore

segments.voice: Yesterday: the chapter of eights, and your line, no view to cling to. Did you ask one real question instead of winning a point? Today, the last poem of that chapter, and it's about fear. Day six hundred eight.

Picture a pond at the end of a long dry season. The water has shrunk to a muddy patch in the middle, and the fish are crowded into it, flapping, pushing against each other for the last of it. That image is at the heart of the final poem of the Atthakavagga, Sutta Nipata 4.15. And unlike most discourses, this one is spoken in the first person. The speaker tells us what he saw, and how it shook him, before he ever found peace. Today: fear from the rod.
screen: `A POND AT THE END OF THE DRY SEASON.` → `FISH CROWDED IN THE MUD.` → `SPOKEN IN THE FIRST PERSON.`

segments.voice: The poem opens with one line that could stand alone: fear is born from the one who takes up the rod. Atta danda, the rod taken up, the stick picked up to strike. Look at people quarreling, the speaker says. And then he describes his own alarm. I saw people trembling, he says, like fish in little water, set against one another, and fear came into me. The world seemed to have no core; every direction was shaken. I looked for a place for myself and found none that wasn't already claimed. Seeing everyone in conflict to the end, I was disturbed. Then the turn. I saw a dart, he says, hard to see, lodged in the heart. Pulled along by that dart, people run in every direction. Pull it out, and you don't run, and you don't sink. Two things are worth holding. First, the line about the rod cuts both ways. The one who picks up the stick creates fear in others, and also lives in fear. Second, the cause isn't finally the other fish. It's the dart inside, the craving and grasping, that makes the pond feel so small. Commentaries set the poem during a quarrel between two clans, the Sakyans and the Koliyans, over the water of a river. The poem itself names no one.
screen: `THE ONE WHO TAKES UP THE ROD.` · `FISH IN LITTLE WATER.` · `NO PLACE NOT ALREADY CLAIMED.` · `A DART HARD TO SEE.` · then, large: `FEAR BORN FROM THE ROD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see one quarrel's root. Sit and settle. Bring to mind a conflict you're part of, large or small: a sibling, a neighbor, a group chat. Picture the shrinking pond. What is the patch of water you're both fighting for? Being right, being respected, being safe? Then look for the dart in your own chest, the wanting that keeps you flapping. Don't pull hard. Just see it. Then let the breath settle around it. The bell holds the time.
Attadanda, the rod taken up. The opening of Sutta Nipata 4.15: whoever takes up the stick to strike breeds fear, in others and in themselves. Today's word.
Your line: fear born from the rod. Today, when you feel like picking up a stick, a sharp email, a cold shoulder, notice the fear that comes with it, and set it down. Day six hundred eight.

howItsDone: Teachers in several Buddhist traditions read the Attadanda Sutta as an account of the urgency, or samvega, that turns a person toward practice, and it is often cited in teaching on nonviolence.

fork.setup: you look out and see everyone in conflict, crowding like fish in a shrinking pond, and fear comes over you. what does the speaker of Sn 4.15 find next?
options: a dart, hard to see, lodged in the heart.
fork.reveal: he sees the hidden dart that drives people every which way. pull it out, the poem says, and one neither runs nor sinks.

original.note: Pali attadanda: the rod taken up, the title of Sn 4.15. danda is a stick or rod.

trapdoor: what you thought: people pick up sticks because they're afraid.
what it means: the poem says fear is born from taking up the stick, in those threatened and in the one who threatens.
what a scholar hears: Sn 4.15 is a rare first-person account of samvega, the shock that leads to the path; the commentary sets it at the Rohini river quarrel.
recall: a monk who had been a wandering poet

notes: Sn 4.15 paraphrased. Confirm the first-person sequence: fish in little water, the world without core, no place unclaimed, the dart hard to see.
The commentary's setting (Sakyans and Koliyans quarreling over the Rohini river) is given as tradition; confirm.
Note that 'atta' in attadanda is read by most as 'taken up' (atta from adatti), not 'self'; confirm the gloss.
